A returning colony is using entries that survived the last attempt — on layered historic rooflines there are usually several: fascia gaps, junction openings, a gable vent with a torn screen. Lincolnton.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Lincolnton in Lincoln County, where western Piedmont west of Lake Norman puts woods and water right against housing. Raccoons den in chimneys and attics in spring, squirrels chew soffits year-round, and bats use older rooflines in summer.

Most Lincolnton jobs start with a full roofline, attic, and crawlspace inspection, then removal and sealing as one job, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Lincolnton is a courthouse city with its history intact — a historic downtown of brick commercial blocks and church streets, older neighbourhoods under big oaks, and the South Fork of the Catawba River bending along its edge. Its wildlife work is old-city work: bats in the tall attics and behind the fascia of the historic homes, raccoons in the chimneys, gray squirrels in the canopy streets, and rats in the older commercial roofs along Main Street. The river bottoms and the county's farmland press in from both sides, and the beaver work along the South Fork's tributaries is a standing item for the low properties.

East Lincoln's growth toward Lake Norman has changed the county faster than the city — but inside Lincolnton the pattern stays historic: layered rooflines, additions on additions, crawlspaces under pier-built homes, and porches that have been enclosed, opened, and enclosed again across a century. Every one of those junctions is a door until somebody closes it in metal, and our Lincolnton inspections assume the doors are there until the read proves otherwise.
Lincolnton.extendedBody:
Historic rooflines and the full-entry read

Lincolnton's older homes concentrate their risk at the junctions: where the porch roof meets the wall, where the addition's roof dies into the original, at the gable vents and the chimney flashing. Squirrels chew in at the softwood junctions; bats take the fascia gaps too small to see from the ground; raccoons use the failures both leave behind. We seal in metal fitted to the old framing and map every entry — on a historic Lincolnton home, sealing the found entry without the full read is how a colony becomes a tradition. Our operators are licensed Wildlife Control Agents with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission, and removal runs through the depredation-permit system, the permit issued for your property forming the job's legal basis.

The South Fork bottoms

Along the South Fork and its tributaries, the ground work runs wet: beaver dams in the drainage backing water toward the low streets, bank burrows, and the raccoon and opossum traffic the bottoms carry into town nightly. Low properties get a water pass with the house inspection. And over everything, the state bat calendar: North Carolina prohibits evictions during pup season, May 1 through July 31 — Lincolnton's attic colonies are mapped in the window and excluded completely from August, all entries at once.

Commercial Main Street

The older commercial blocks carry their own log — Norway rats in the roof voids and wall systems, pigeons in the sign structures and parapets. Commercial work is building work: entries found and sealed at the structure, with the neighbouring buildings' role stated honestly, because a rat population on a historic block belongs to the block until several buildings close at once.

Crouse.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Crouse in Lincoln County, where western Piedmont west of Lake Norman puts woods and water right against housing. Raccoons den in chimneys and attics in spring, squirrels chew soffits year-round, and bats use older rooflines in summer.

Most Crouse jobs start with a full roofline, attic, and crawlspace inspection, then removal and sealing as one job, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Crouse is Lincoln County's quiet corner — an unincorporated farming community of crossroads churches, farmhouses, and newer homes spread along the rural roads west of Lincolnton, in rolling piedmont where Indian Creek and the farm branches cut the fields. No downtown, no subdivisions to speak of: Crouse's wildlife work is the pure farmstead version. Raccoons in the barn lofts and farmhouse chimneys, groundhogs in the field banks and under the outbuildings, skunks under every porch, opossums in the well houses, and bats in the older homes' attics — with the creek bottoms carrying beaver work to the low farms after wet winters.

Distance shapes the service pattern here. Crouse properties are far apart and far from town, so a half-job is an expensive habit: the visit that inspects only the house and misses the barn means a second trip and a raccoon that spent the interval in the loft. Our Crouse work is planned as whole-farmstead surveys from the first call — every structure on the parcel read in one pass, removal and sealing sequenced across them, so the property is finished rather than visited.
Crouse.extendedBody:
One visit, whole farmstead

The Crouse standard is a single comprehensive pass: house attic and chimney, barn lofts, well house, equipment sheds, and the fence-line banks, ranked by activity and handled in an order that leaves the animals no structure to rotate into. Raccoons are the usual residents — denning in lofts, taking chimneys in spring — with opossums and skunks in the ground-level voids. Removal runs through North Carolina's depredation-permit system, and every operator is a licensed Wildlife Control Agent with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission; on a rural property that permit paperwork is part of the job's legitimacy, and we are glad to show it.

Groundhogs in horse and cattle country

Crouse's ground constant is the groundhog: burrow systems in the pasture banks, along the creek terraces, and under barn foundations — a livestock hazard in working fields, not a garden nuisance. We trap the animals working the ground and collapse or screen the active entrances in the grazed areas, walking the fence lines with the owner because the burrows that matter are the ones in the animals' paths. Bats follow the state calendar overhead: no evictions during pup season, May 1 through July 31, so farmhouse colonies are mapped in summer and excluded completely from August.

Creek bottoms and wet-year beavers

Indian Creek and the farm branches run slow through Crouse's low ground, and in wet years beavers dam them and back water over the bottom fields and crossings. Beaver work here is the reach treated whole — animals, dam, and water level together — with a spring re-check as the standing pattern for bottom properties.
